data.title: Top Chinese official leads 87-member committee for Tung Chee-hwa state funeral
data.description:
The first vice-chairman of the nation’s top political advisory body is overseeing an 87-member committee of political and business heavyweights to arrange the state funeral for Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa.
A vigil will be held from 3pm to 10pm on Saturday at the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point and a public memorial service will start at 9am on Sunday, according to an obituary placed by Tung’s family in the South China Morning Post on Tuesday.
“In lieu of flowers, please make donations to charities of your choice,” the obituary read.
Details of the state funeral were also announced in an advertisement published in the SCMP, with Shi Taifeng, Politburo member and top vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), heading the funeral committee.
The committee has four deputy directors: Wang Dongfeng, a member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China and CPPCC vice-chairman and secretary general; Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO); John Lee Ka-chiu, the head of the city; and predecessor Leung Chun-ying.
The remaining 82 members include tycoons, political and business leaders from Hong Kong and mainland China. Among them are: Wang Yonghong, deputy secretary general of the State Council and a Central Committee member; Zhou Ji, liaison office director; Dong Jingwei, head of Beijing’s Office for Safeguarding National Security in Hong Kong; and local foreign ministry chief Cui Jianchun.
Other members are billionaire businessmen Li Ka-shing, Peter Woo Kwong-ching, Henry Cheng Kar-shun and Peter Lee Ka-kit, former Macau chief executive Edmund Ho Hau-wah, former secretary for justice Elsie Leung Oi-sie, former Legislative Council presidents Jasper Tsang Yok-sing and Rita Fan Hsu Lai-tai and ex-chief executive of Bank of East Asia David Li Kwok-po.
Also on the list are former city leaders Donald Tsang Yam-kuen and Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor, former chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority Joseph Yam Chi-kwong and president of the Legislative Council Starry Lee Wai-king, who is also Hong Kong’s sole delegate to China’s top legislative body, the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress.
Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok, Chief Justice Andrew Cheung Kui-nung and various legislators are also committee members.
The SCMP previously reported that Tung would be honoured with a state funeral for his service as a deputy national-level leader and his contributions to the “one country, two systems” governing framework.
The former city leader died peacefully in hospital with family members by his side last Tuesday at the age of 89.

Following his death, Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong issued a statement describing Tung as a “close friend of the Communist Party of China”, an “outstanding contributor to one country, two systems” and a “renowned patriot”.
Since the 1997 handover, only two other local figures have been granted state funerals: industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006.
Similar to Tung, both served as vice-chairs of the CPPCC.
The state funerals of Ann and Fok were coordinated by the central government, with the committees handling the arrangements each chaired by a CPPCC vice-chairman. The committee for Ann’s funeral had 65 people, while Fok’s had 74.
Both funerals were also attended by senior mainland Chinese officials, including the HKMAO director, with the coffins draped in the national flag and state leaders laying wreaths in tribute.
Ann, a textile entrepreneur, was regarded as one of a handful of capitalists who had the ear of Chinese president Deng Xiaoping in the early 1980s and held key positions in major bodies that Beijing formed to prepare for the handover.
Tung and Fok served as two of the eight pallbearers at Ann’s funeral at the Hong Kong Funeral Home after he died of heart complications at 88. Ann was buried in Dapengwan Cemetery in Shenzhen.
The other pallbearers at the time included both mainland and local officials, including Leung, as well as the late entertainment tycoon Run Run Shaw and two of Ann’s long-time business partners.
Fok, a tycoon with gambling, port and property interests, died on October 28, 2006, in Beijing at the age of 83 after a long battle with cancer. His coffin was flown to Hong Kong several days later in accordance with his wishes to be buried back home.
His funeral was also held at the Hong Kong Funeral Home. He was buried at the Hong Kong Buddhist Cemetery in Chai Wan.
Headed by Wang Zhongyu, a CPPCC vice-chairman at the time, the committee for Fok’s funeral had four deputy directors: then HKMAO director Liao Hui; Liu Yandong, head of the United Front Work Department at the time; Tung; and then chief executive Donald Tsang Yam-kuen.
As Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung played a pivotal role in implementing the then-untested and novel one country, two systems model, under which the city has been administered since the end of British colonial rule in 1997.
After resigning as city leader in March 2005 for health reasons, Tung went on to assume a prominent role at the national level and increasingly came to be regarded as an elder statesman.

data.title: Wrise Prestige accelerates mainland China expansion with new offices, AI lab
data.description:
Wealth management provider Wrise Prestige is stepping up its investment in artificial intelligence technology as the firm looks to expand its footprint on the Chinese mainland and power its next phase of growth.
The Singapore-headquartered firm planned to open an AI laboratory in Guangzhou next month to house its technology team, following a HK$30 million internal investment in AI-related development, senior executives said during a media briefing marking the company’s second anniversary in Hong Kong on Tuesday.
The initiative will focus on building enterprise systems and streamlining operational efficiency across the group, with further capital expenditure planned for future tech initiatives, according to the company.
Henry Shin, the company’s chief executive, said the plan aimed to merge technology with professional expertise rather than replace human advisers.
“AI is meant to empower our business operations and elevate service efficiency, but the human wealth consultant remains the absolute core of our client relationships,” Shin said.
The firm is moving from an “independent wealth consultant” to an “intelligent wealth consultant” model, according to Shin, which pairs human judgment with AI-driven research and analytics.
“Independence remains a core pillar of the business,” Shin added, stressing that technology allowed advisers to objectively help clients select and design financial solutions.
The initiative aligns with a broader push across Hong Kong’s financial sector to integrate AI into wealth management and capital markets.
Trillions of yuan in wealth will undergo intergenerational transfer in the domestic market in the coming years
Henry Shin, Wrise Prestige
Regulators have been encouraging responsible adoption while urging financial institutions to prepare for a coming wave of autonomous systems. Earlier this month, a senior official at the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) noted at an industry event that the watchdog was considering further regulatory guidance for financial firms deploying autonomous “agentic” AI systems.
The company said its Hong Kong business had expanded rapidly since launching in 2024, with assets under management rising 927 per cent, revenue increasing 301 per cent and client numbers growing 382 per cent compared with the end of 2024. Its network has grown to more than 400 wealth consultants.
Beyond Hong Kong, the group was expanding its mainland presence with offices in Shenzhen, Chengdu, Changsha and Wuxi, focusing on investor outreach, research and family office education, the executives said.
“Trillions of yuan in wealth will undergo intergenerational transfer in the domestic market in the coming years,” Shin said, pointing to rising demand for succession planning and advisory services.
The expansion comes as Hong Kong reinforces its position as a global hub for private wealth. Total assets under management in the city’s private banking and wealth management sector rose 24 per cent year on year to HK$12.9 trillion at the end of 2025, according to SFC data.

data.title: Hong Kong finance chief urges Cathay to keep fares attractive, add routes
data.description:
Hong Kong’s finance chief has called on Cathay Pacific Airways to offer attractive fares and expand its route network, as China’s national development plan reinforces the city’s status as a global aviation hub.
Speaking at Cathay’s 80th anniversary celebration on Tuesday, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po described the flag carrier as more than just a transport provider, calling it an ambassador for Hong Kong that reinforced the city’s status as a global aviation hub and “superconnector”.
Chan emphasised that each new route drove trade, investment and economic opportunities, noting that bringing people together and unlocking new markets was especially vital in an uncertain global climate.
He said that the three-runway system at Hong Kong International Airport – now nearly two years operational – provided more capacity for growth, adding that the government was pursuing new air services agreements and expanded traffic rights in such markets as the Middle East, Central Asia, Africa and South America.
“As the government opens the way for wider air links, I encourage Cathay to seize these opportunities and add new destinations to your network,” Chan said. “I am sure passengers would be delighted to see one more thing: your excellent service accompanied by equally attractive fares. Guy and Ronald, I shall leave that in your capable hands,” he added, addressing Cathay Group chairman Guy Bradley and CEO Ronald Lam Siu-por.
At the same event, Bradley highlighted that the group now operated scheduled passenger services to more than 100 destinations worldwide – including 24 in mainland China – via Cathay and its low-cost carrier, HK Express.
He said the group planned to expand into more belt and road destinations, including Almaty, Kazakhstan, next January.
He was referring to participating nations in the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s project to build a China-centred global trading network.
“In the next 10 years, we target to have 150 new aircraft join our fleet, and build a network serving 150 destinations worldwide, if market conditions are favourable,” Bradley said.

Chan acknowledged that Cathay’s 80-year history included “difficult chapters”, recalling the Covid-19 pandemic period when the government led a HK$39 billion recapitalisation package for the airline in 2020.
“During the pandemic, the government’s support reflected our determination to safeguard Hong Kong’s status as an international aviation hub and our confidence in Cathay’s role within it,” he said. “That was an investment in our shared future. And it was your people – their professionalism, perseverance and dedication – who helped turn confidence into recovery.
“Your work matters far beyond air connections. For Hong Kong, every new route is another opening for trade, investment and opportunity. This is our ‘superconnector’ role in practice: bringing businesses to markets, and people to one another.
“In an uncertain world, we must pursue these opportunities with prudence as well as confidence,” Chan said. “The case for bringing people together and opening up new markets is stronger, not weaker.”
He said Cathay’s commitment of about HK$150 billion (US$19.12 billion) to investments in aircraft, cabins, lounges and digital innovation was a vote of confidence in Hong Kong’s future.
“The national 15th five-year plan explicitly supports Hong Kong in consolidating and enhancing our status as an international aviation hub,” he said. “We are determined to translate that support into greater capacity, wider reach and lasting economic benefits.”

data.title: Tighter scrutiny of Hong Kong IPOs could slow deal flow, analysts say
data.description:
Securities regulators in Hong Kong and mainland China are doubling down on efforts to raise the quality of Hong Kong initial public offerings (IPOs), which could slow the flow of new listings but would not reduce underlying demand, according to analysts.
In an unusual move, the China Securities Regulatory Commission recently asked nine mainland companies, which had already been pre-approved for listings, to provide supplementary materials detailing fund usage, shareholding structures and pending litigation.
Hong Kong’s market watchdog, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), on Thursday directed the city’s bourse operator to suspend trading of US-based biotech firm Cloudbreak Pharma, explicitly expressing concerns that the company’s IPO could have been “rigged” to create an artificial impression of demand.
“The launch of new projects has been affected,” said Hang Wang, chief representative of Baker McKenzie’s Beijing office and co-chair of its China capital markets practice, when asked about the regulator actions. “This has pushed mainstream investment banks to become more cautious when screening projects and potential clients.”
This “tightening of quality oversight” would have a knock-on effect on intermediaries including law firms, auditors and industry advisers, which would lead to a reduction in the number of new projects being screened and launched, he added.
In another recent case, the SFC instructed Futu Securities to freeze up to HK$125.2 million (US$16 million) in client assets linked to suspected artificial demand creation in July.
Listing activity in the city’s stock market is running unusually hot, with hundreds of mainland AI, robotics and tech companies lining up to debut. At least 500 companies had submitted applications, excluding confidential filings, according to bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX).

In the first eight months of 2026, companies raised HK$651 billion through IPOs and secondary placements in Hong Kong, with IPOs accounting for about HK$342 billion.
“Every time the IPO market is hot, some substandard companies try to sneak through,” said Roy Lo Wa Kei, managing partner at accounting and consulting firm SW Hong Kong. “Since regulators stepped in, intermediaries have become much stricter in their gatekeeping.”
The SFC said in a January circular that some listing documents had serious flaws, including a possible lack of thorough understanding of applicants and insufficient due diligence. It now limits signing sponsors to handling five deals at a time.
Lo said the watchdog would strengthen sponsors’ due diligence duties, covering client knowledge, legal, intellectual property and financial checks.
He also said he expected more guidance to be released soon on valuation reasonableness, so that high valuations for AI and new economy firms would no longer rely on companies “blowing their own trumpet”.
Despite these hurdles, Baker McKenzie’s Wang said the city was not trying to raise listing thresholds or shut companies out.
“HKEX remains committed to simplifying the listing process and lowering barriers, and continues to welcome strong companies to list in Hong Kong,” he said.
The bourse operator implemented its most ambitious listing reform in eight years in July, significantly lowering the financial and market capitalisation thresholds for companies with weighted voting rights and allowing all new applicants to submit listing applications confidentially.
“This may seem at odds with stricter quality oversight, but it isn’t,” Wang said. “HKEX is essentially trading quantity for quality. Regulators care more about bringing in high-quality companies with real investment value than about simply racking up the number of listed companies.”
Underlying market demand had “never truly halted”, he added.
“Taking our firm’s daily operations as an example, we continue to pitch to prospective clients and hold kick-off meetings each month. Overall, the Hong Kong IPO market is shifting towards a healthier, more manageable and sustainable trajectory.”

data.title: Mainland Chinese joint venture launches new electric taxi in Hong Kong
data.description:
A mainland Chinese joint venture will introduce an electric taxi in Hong Kong next month, but a lawmaker has warned that a lack of quick-charging stations remains the biggest challenge to the government’s target of introducing 3,000 such cabs by next year.
SAIC-GM-Wuling, a joint venture between SAIC Motor, General Motors China and Guangxi Automobile Group, on Tuesday unveiled its Darion Taxi, a new six-seater e-taxi to be launched in Hong Kong.
DH Legend Motors, the joint venture’s sole Hong Kong distributor, expects to deliver the new model next month.
Wong Kin-man, the distributor’s director and general manager, said the model had a 540km (336-mile) range and 30-minute quick-charging capacity, designed to meet demand in the city.
“We promise to provide car owners and drivers across Hong Kong with the highest quality, most professional factory maintenance and repair services,” Wong said.
“Our team will continuously strive for faster, better and more efficient after-sales support, significantly shorten repair waiting times to ensure smooth taxi operations across Hong Kong and give drivers peace of mind in making a living.”
He said the new model would come with a 500,000km battery warranty and cost about HK$300,000 (US$38,248), adding that he expected the company to sell at least 300 cars.
Wong added the company would also build Hong Kong’s largest battery repair centre next year, which would cut battery repair costs by about 60 per cent.

Wong Po-keung, chairman of the Hong Kong Taxi Owners’ Association, said the new model’s quick-charging capacity was attractive to taxi owners.
The vehicle’s real-world range could be closer to 400km once factors such as Hong Kong’s traffic congestion and air conditioning use were taken into account, he added.
The Environment and Ecology Bureau said Hong Kong had 988 electric taxis in 2025, which accounted for a fraction of the city’s total of about 18,000 cabs.
The government has set a target of introducing 3,000 electric taxis by 2027.
Lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung said the biggest challenge to hitting the target remained the lack of quick-charging facilities for electric vehicles.
He noted that the government was relying on the market to solve the problem, but called for authorities to introduce more quick charging stations specifically for taxis.
“Many taxi [drivers] need to charge their cars within a short time – about an hour while having their meals – and they cover a lot of mileage every day. They can only provide service if they’re able to charge to a full battery [during these intervals],” he said.
Chong suggested that the government set up more fast chargers at the airport, Disneyland and other tourist spots, adding that such facilities could also help divert traffic at gas stations for petrol and gas-powered taxis.

data.title: China is beating the US in consumer AI adoption, thanks to super apps: report
data.description:
China is surging ahead of the US in consumer AI adoption as technology giants like Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding embed artificial intelligence directly into popular everyday apps, even as American models lead in capability, according to Morgan Stanley.
A survey conducted by the bank and published in a report on Monday showed that 80 per cent of Chinese respondents used AI for personal purposes at least weekly, compared with 54 per cent in the US.
China’s generative AI user base grew from about 249 million in December 2024 to 602 million in December 2025, scaling significantly faster than mobile internet adoption did over a comparable period, the report said.
While basic access to AI remained free in both nations, China’s advantage stemmed from distributing services through everyday platforms tailored to local consumer habits, rather than holding an edge in frontier model benchmark performance, Morgan Stanley noted.
In China, generative AI functions – capable of producing text, images, video or code – are embedded directly into shopping, search, messaging and entertainment apps, allowing users to leverage AI without downloading stand-alone software.
ByteDance’s Doubao, which received traffic from TikTok’s Chinese sibling Douyin, has emerged as the clear leader among native AI apps, reaching about 399 million monthly active users (MAU) in July, according to QuestMobile data cited in the report.

It was followed by Alibaba’s Qwen – an AI agent designed to execute real-world tasks by plugging directly into Alibaba’s ecosystem of shopping, travel booking, navigation and payments platforms – with 161 million MAUs.
However, “multi-homing” was becoming the norm, with 64 per cent of surveyed Chinese respondents using five or more AI tools, Morgan Stanley said. The low cost of switching between apps prevented a winner-take-all situation for stand-alone apps and favoured existing platforms that control user demand, proprietary data and transactions, according to the bank.
As a result, incumbents with strong distribution networks were best positioned to benefit, according to Morgan Stanley. Tencent, in particular, was likely to see its WeChat ecosystem of social graphs, mini-programmes and payments enhanced rather than displaced by native AI tools.
Alibaba remained a top stock pick for the bank for its full-stack capabilities, particularly in-app commerce features like Taobao’s Qwen shopping assistant, though analysts remained cautious about investments in the stand-alone Qwen app.
Meituan and online travel agencies were also well-positioned because of their high conversion efficiency at low incremental acquisition costs.
Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

data.title: Man arrested after HK$1 million in gems stolen from hotel guest asleep in lobby
data.description:
Hong Kong police have arrested a man and recovered uncut gemstones worth nearly HK$1 million (US$127,500) that were allegedly snatched from an overseas businessman as he slept in a hotel lobby.
The force said on Monday that the suspected theft happened a day earlier while the businessman, a 29-year-old jeweller from Sri Lanka, was in the city for the “Jewellery & Gem World Hong Kong September” trade fair.
The jewellery was allegedly taken from the victim as he slept in the lobby, where he was waiting to check in at a hotel near Hong Kong International Airport.
Police said the suspect was believed to have taken advantage of the situation to search the businessman’s backpack placed on his luggage and removed a batch of uncut gemstones valued at nearly HK$1 million before fleeing.
Airport district officers launched an investigation and identified the suspect with the help of the surveillance footage collected by the force.
About six hours later, officers arrested a 32-year-old Algerian man at a hotel in Tsing Yi, with the precious stones recovered intact.
Police are investigating whether the suspect had any accomplices.
The force reminded the public to safeguard personal belongings, noting that with the jewellery exhibition under way, officers had stepped up patrols and intelligence monitoring to deter crime.
It also urged exhibitors to remain vigilant, keep an eye on their valuables and avoid disclosing storage locations for their items.

data.title: 85% of Wang Fuk Court owners sign sale deals as flat selection moves ahead
data.description:
More than 85 per cent of owners at the blaze-hit Wang Fuk Court have signed agreements to sell their flats to the Hong Kong government as authorities move ahead with flat selection under a special rehousing scheme.
Authorities said on Tuesday that 1,702 households – 85.8 per cent of flat owners across blocks A to H at the estate – had signed sale and purchase agreements as of Monday.
On the same day, the bureau held computerised draws to determine the selection sequence for subsidised flats under the scheme.
“The Housing Bureau conducted separate computerised random-ordering ballots for the two batches of applicants to determine the sequence of the last two digits of the application numbers held by the applicants,” a spokesman said. “Based on the ballot results, the Housing Bureau randomly generated the order of all applicants.”
In the wake of the blaze last November, which killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000, the government announced a buy-back of all 1,984 flats at the subsidised housing estate in Tai Po.
Under the scheme, flats are being acquired at HK$8,000 (US$1,020) or HK$10,500 per square foot depending on whether owners have paid the land premium.
Participating owners can use the cash compensation to purchase a flat on the private open market or join a special sales exercise to buy new subsidised housing under a flat-for-flat arrangement.
Owners had until August 31 to submit acceptance letters. Those who indicated their intention to sell by June 30 are eligible for priority flat selection.
The bureau said flat selection under the special sales exercise was expected to commence later this month.
“The Housing Bureau will, in accordance with the order of priority, issue letters in batches to notify applicants of the priority order and invite eligible applicants to attend flat selection sessions,” a bureau spokesman said.

Ballot results and the priority order based on the computerised draw have been uploaded to the designated website, the bureau added.
The government has set aside more than 4,400 flats at 10 development projects for these owners, spread across Kowloon Bay, Kai Tak, Kam Tin, Tseung Kwan O, Ping Shan, Tung Chung, Tai Po, Fanling and Kwun Tong.
Earlier, the South China Morning Post spoke to six residents who said they would not sell, arguing that no financial package could compensate for the loss of their long-time homes and community ties.

data.title: Chinese carmakers GAC and FAW eye potential tie-up of their Toyota operations
data.description:
Two Chinese state-owned carmakers, Guangzhou Automobile Group (GAC) and FAW Group, are weighing a restructuring that could integrate their joint venture operations with Japanese giant Toyota, industry insiders say, following Beijing’s call for consolidation amid weakening domestic demand.
GAC planned to acquire part of FAW’s equity in a joint venture vehicle manufacturer through a share issuance and raise supporting funds, the Guangzhou-based carmaker said in an exchange filing on Monday night, following a full-day trading halt.
The target asset involved a foreign-listed company, but GAC did not disclose its name or the deal value. The deal remained in the planning stage, subject to internal approvals and regulatory clearance, GAC said.
Analysts and mainland media reports said the target company was FAW’s joint venture with Toyota.
“From a strategic and synergy perspective, a Toyota-related target is more likely,” said Claire Yuan, director of corporate ratings for China autos at S&P Global Ratings, in a reply to the South China Morning Post.
“This transaction could resolve the long-standing competition between GAC-Toyota and FAW-Toyota.”
Yuan added it would mark a critical move for state-owned enterprises, which had largely lagged in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs).
GAC has joint ventures with Toyota and Honda, while FAW – which is controlled directly by the central government – partners with Toyota, Volkswagen and Audi.
The deal is expected to set an important precedent for cross-regional consolidation among central and local carmakers
China International Capital Corporation
The deal aimed to “promote the optimal integration of industrial resources among local and central state-owned enterprises, and enhance operational efficiency of listed companies,” GAC said in the filing.
Investment bank China International Capital Corporation said in a research note on Tuesday that if the restructuring went through, it was “expected to set an important precedent for cross-regional consolidation among central and local carmakers, send a positive signal of ‘anti-involution’, and help improve market sentiment”.
Involution, or neijuan, refers to excessive competition, where more resources are invested without increasing returns or reinvestment in research and development.
GAC’s Hong Kong-listed shares closed 2.6 per cent higher on Tuesday. Trading in its Shanghai shares remained suspended.
The announcement followed a pledge by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology – China’s industrial watchdog – and eight other agencies on Friday to intensify efforts to promote mergers, reorganisations and cross-regional integration among carmakers, while advancing reforms towards group-based management.
Despite strong exports, China’s domestic vehicle sales have slowed sharply after years of rapid growth and subsidy withdrawal, squeezing profitability.
Retail sales fell 20.8 per cent year on year to 11.7 million units in the first eight months of the year, while profit margins shrank by 1 percentage point to 3.6 per cent in the January-July period, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed.
Joint ventures between local and foreign carmakers, which once dominated the mainland market, have struggled amid China’s rapid shift towards EVs.
In August, joint venture retail sales of petrol-powered cars and EVs plunged 35 per cent year on year to some 310,000 units, accounting for just 4.3 per cent of China’s EV market, according to CPCA.
Squeezed by domestic EV makers like BYD, GAC’s net loss in the first half of the year widened 76 per cent year on year to 4.5 billion yuan (US$670 million).

data.title: Forget AI KPIs: how China’s tech giants are rationing tokens for employees
data.description:
When generative artificial intelligence first swept through China’s technology sector, workers faced a clear directive from management: use AI and use it often.
Consuming vast numbers of AI tokens – the basic unit of computing power needed to process text or write code – became a badge of honour, with companies often viewing a high token count as a sign that employees were productive and taking initiative.
But those computing allowances are now being sharply rolled back as China’s leading internet companies introduce token quotas to rein in rising AI-related costs, according to staff who spoke with the South China Morning Post on condition of anonymity.
At ByteDance, one employee said staff using closed-source models must co-pay out of pocket. The company reimburses roughly half of external tool costs, capping annual payouts at around US$1,000 for technical staff and interns, and US$300 for non-technical employees, according to the staff member.
Alibaba Group Holding, meanwhile, allocates employees 3,000 to 6,000 monthly credits for its internal coding platform, QoderWork, with additional credits granted when needed, according to people familiar with the programme. Reimbursements for external AI tools are capped at US$200 a month and subject to security rules.
At Baidu, developers start with a baseline allowance of 1,500 yuan (US$223) a month, with another 1,500 yuan top-up available upon request, according to employees.
While routine development tasks typically only consumed about 500 yuan worth of tokens per month, staff using advanced models in “deep-thinking” modes could exhaust their monthly allowance much more quickly, they said.


At Tencent Holdings, workers who previously had access to flat annual token allocations must now draw from departmental pools overseen by line managers, according to several employees.
Those who ran out mid-month had to file requests with their supervisors for additional resources, the sources said. Tencent has reassured employees that it would not rank them by token consumption nor measure their performance solely by token usage.
In response to queries, Tencent said on Saturday that it aimed to meet employee AI token needs as far as possible, adjusting allocations based on workload, demand and model capabilities. The company added that “tokenmaxxing” – excessive consumption merely to inflate usage numbers – should not be encouraged.
Alibaba, Baidu and ByteDance did not respond to requests for comment. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
The tightening rules reflect an operational headache brewing inside tech firms. As workers adopt increasingly complex agentic AI workflows – where software autonomously plans, executes code, searches for information and verifies its own work – a single prompt can rapidly burn through computational capacity.
Data from Goldman Sachs highlights the scale of the demand. Enterprise and consumer token consumption was projected to jump 24-fold between 2026 and 2030, reaching 120 quadrillion tokens monthly, the bank said in a May report.
While the cost to process each token was forecast to fall by 60 to 70 per cent annually, lower prices could encourage companies to run models more frequently, analysts said.
Additional reporting by Ann Cao, Ben Jiang and Coco Feng

data.title: Hong Kong visitor arrivals hit post-pandemic monthly high in August
data.description:
Hong Kong recorded its highest monthly number of visitors since the Covid-19 pandemic in August, provisional official figures show, with authorities attributing the surge to a series of international conferences and mega-events.
The Hong Kong Tourism Board said on Tuesday that the city received 5.46 million visitors across the month, up by 6 per cent from a year earlier and the highest monthly total since the pandemic.
Tourist numbers in the first eight months of the year also rose by 11 per cent year on year, fuelled by an influx of mainland Chinese and long-haul international arrivals.
The board attributed the increase in August to international conferences and mega-events held during the month, including the 16th Worldwide Chinese Life Insurance Congress & 2026 IDA Annual Conference, the Hong Kong Football Festival 2026 and the TMElive International Music Awards.
“[They] attracted a diverse range of visitors and helped drive visitor arrivals from the Chinese mainland, Singapore, the United Kingdom and other source markets,” it said.
Provisional figures released by the board showed that nearly 4.6 million of the August arrivals came from the mainland, an 8 per cent increase from a year earlier.
Long-haul arrivals also rose by 18 per cent year on year to 289,489, while visitors from new markets increased by 10 per cent to more than 65,000.

Short-haul visitors from outside the mainland were the only segment to decline, falling by 16 per cent to about 405,000.
For the first eight months of the year, Hong Kong welcomed 36.7 million visitors, 11 per cent more than in the same period last year. More than 28.7 million came from the mainland, representing growth of 13 per cent.
The city also received about 4 million short-haul visitors during the period, down by 4 per cent year on year, while long-haul arrivals rose by 19 per cent to 2.6 million.
Visitors from new markets reached 550,000, an increase of 15 per cent.
The tourism board said the performance of the mainland and long-haul markets had remained stable.
“Visitor growth in short-haul markets continued to face challenges owing to factors such as flight capacity, fuel surcharges and regional competition,” it said.
The board added that it would step up promotion for Hong Kong’s celebrations for Chinese and Western festivals, including the “International Lantern Spectacular”, which will feature displays from 20 countries at Victoria Park to mark the Mid-Autumn Festival, as well as the city’s Halloween events.
It also highlighted coming flagship events, including the Hong Kong Cyclothon, Hong Kong Wine & Dine Festival and New Year countdown celebrations, as further draws for tourists.
“[The board] will continue to join hands with partners across the tourism and business sectors to promote ‘Only in Hong Kong’ tourism experiences, attracting more high-value-added overnight visitors and driving the economy through tourism,” it said.

data.title: Chinese researchers chart 5-stage path toward ‘last AI built by humans’
data.description:
Researchers from China’s leading universities and tech giants are setting their sights on a crucial new front in the AI race with the US: developing systems capable of building better versions of themselves without human intervention.
In a joint paper published on Thursday, researchers from ByteDance, Tsinghua University and the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, among others, outlined a five-stage road map for recursive self-improvement (RSI).
The study, titled “The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement”, highlights a growing industry focus on automating the labour-intensive life cycle of training, evaluating, and fine-tuning AI models.
The paper describes five progressive stages of autonomy. In the initial phase, an AI merely executes improvement procedures designed by human engineers. It then begins to choose how to upgrade itself, rather than simply carrying out preprogrammed instructions.
In later stages, the system determines what new information or experiences it must acquire, adapting to changes post-deployment. The final stage would allow an AI to persistently refine the very methods used to improve AI itself.
Unlike a chatbot correcting an individual response, RSI requires improvements to persist beyond a single task and be inherited by successor systems.
The authors argue that the ability to automate parts of AI research could become a source of competitive advantage for model developers.
If realised, this paradigm shift could shorten development cycles while slashing the labour and computational costs required to build foundation models, according to the authors.

Automating AI research has emerged as a core battleground in US-China technological competition. While Chinese institutions continue to make rapid practical leaps, experts note that US firms maintain an early lead, largely due to superior access to compute resources.
“American companies still appear several months ahead of China and have access to more compute for deployment,” said Erich Grunewald, senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy. “Chinese researchers are very capable at squeezing performance from scarce hardware, but those compute constraints do still bite.”
Despite the challenges, Chinese firms are doubling down on autonomous training infrastructure.
Z.ai, known in China as Zhipu AI, said on Sunday it would allocate about 60 per cent of the net proceeds from its latest US$5 billion fundraising round to support the development of its next-generation GLM foundation models and its “fully self-training system”.
Researchers behind MiniMax 2.7 said in an article titled “Early Echoes of Self-Evolution” earlier this year that the model could update its memory and build complex skills while executing reinforcement-learning experiments, with the resulting experience feeding back into its learning process.
DeepSeek last month developed an agentic “harness” that gives models greater autonomy to navigate multi-step tasks, execute code and interact with external software.
The authors noted in their paper that progression through the five stages would vary widely depending on the AI field. Software engineering presented a relatively clear path forward, whereas robotics and scientific discovery faced steeper hurdles.
Safety remains another major concern. The researchers said that genuine RSI required strict safeguards, including verified testing environments to ensure updates were safe and beneficial before being deployed.
The authors provided no timetable on when RSI could be achieved.

data.title: Hong Kong’s employment outlook rebounds sharply to 14% in fourth quarter
data.description:
Hong Kong employers’ hiring sentiment rebounded sharply for the fourth quarter, with far fewer companies expecting to cut jobs as confidence improved alongside stronger economic growth, according to a ManpowerGroup survey.
The international human resources company said the city’s seasonally adjusted net employment outlook rose to 14 per cent, up 23 percentage points from minus 9 per cent in the previous quarter.
The outlook is calculated by subtracting the percentage of employers expecting to reduce staffing from the share planning to increase headcount.
Among 603 employers surveyed, 30 per cent expected to increase staffing, 16 per cent anticipated cuts and 54 per cent forecast no change.
“If you look at the figures alone, you can see that the economic environment has continued to improve,” said Lancy Chui Yuk-shan, senior vice-president at ManpowerGroup Greater China.
“Thirty per cent of employers plan to increase [their] headcount, compared with 23 per cent last quarter, while the proportion expecting to reduce staff has fallen from 32 per cent to 16 per cent.”
The turnaround was driven not only by more companies planning to hire, but also by a sharp reduction in the number expecting to reduce staffing, she said.
Chui attributed the improvement to a stronger economic backdrop, pointing to Hong Kong’s 5.1 per cent year-on-year real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the first six months of 2026, an upgraded full-year government forecast of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent and unemployment holding at 3.7 per cent.
The information technology sector recorded the strongest hiring outlook at 27 per cent, followed by finance and insurance at 21 per cent, professional, scientific and technical services at 15 per cent and trade and logistics at 10 per cent.
Chui said demand in the technology sector was being driven by the wider adoption of artificial intelligence and corporate digital transformation, with employers particularly seeking workers who could apply AI in business settings alongside skills in data analytics, cloud architecture, cybersecurity and project management.
Financial sector hiring was supported by stronger activity in initial public offerings, asset and wealth management and insurance, with demand expected for investment banking, compliance, fintech, risk management and customer service roles.
Hospitality recorded a net outlook of 5 per cent, with the year-end festive season expected to support recruitment in hotels, catering, retail and customer service.
Manufacturing remained relatively cautious at 7 per cent, with Chui saying much of the hiring involved staff replacement – particularly in technical roles – rather than significant workforce expansion.

Health and social services was the only sector with a negative reading, at minus 3 per cent, although this was still five percentage points higher than in the previous quarter.
Asked whether the rebound could be sustained, Chui said the longer-term trend would depend on the global economic outlook and Hong Kong’s labour market.
Hong Kong’s overall 14 per cent also remained relatively weak compared with the net employment outlook in many other markets, despite the city’s much stronger quarter-on-quarter improvement, she said.
The global fourth-quarter outlook showed the city lagging behind mainland China’s 34 per cent, Vietnam’s 36 per cent and India’s 54 per cent, although it was still ahead of Singapore’s 13 per cent.

data.title: 2 socially isolated brothers found dead in Hong Kong flat, no foul play suspected
data.description:
Two brothers in their fifties have been found dead in their Hong Kong flat, police have said, with a source noting that they had social avoidance tendencies and had been financially supported by their parents.
The exact causes of the deaths have yet to be confirmed by postmortem examinations. No suspicious circumstances had been identified at this stage, the force said on Tuesday.
The bodies were discovered after the elder sister of the two men made a police report on Monday, an insider said.
The sister had been alerted earlier that day by a security guard at Tung Yip House, Lei Tung Estate, who noticed an unusual odour coming from the flat. The guard knocked on the door but received no response.
Police, firefighters and paramedics arrived at the scene and forced open the metal gate and wooden door. They found the decomposing bodies of the two men in the toilet and on the top bunk of a bedroom, respectively.
The men, aged 53 and 55, were pronounced dead at the scene at 2.45pm. Investigators estimated that one brother had died within a week, while the other had died several weeks earlier. The pair lived together.
No suspicious injuries were found on either man, and their identities as Hong Kong residents were confirmed through their identity cards.
Valuables, including HK$10,000 in cash, were left untouched and there were no signs of a struggle. The flat’s letterbox contained letters dated after July 2, while opened letters dated before July 1 were found on the dining table. No medical documents were found, according to the source.
There were no CCTV cameras inside the flat and a review of footage from the building also yielded no useful information, the source added.

Both brothers were unemployed. The younger brother had acted as the elder brother’s sole carer since 2003, while the pair relied on an automatic monthly bank transfer of HK$17,000 from their parents to cover their living expenses, the insider said.
The sister told police that neither brother had received a formal medical diagnosis.
But she said the elder brother had displayed a severe tendency towards social withdrawal since birth, rarely spoke to anyone, including family members, and went to great lengths to avoid social interaction.
He left school after Form Four and worked as a technician at a power station for about a year before becoming unemployed and relying on his younger brother for financial support, according to the source.
The younger brother had also displayed mild introverted tendencies since childhood. He left school after Form Four, worked as a goldsmith for several years and later stopped working, becoming financially dependent on his parents.
The sister last confirmed that the younger brother was in good health at a family gathering on February 18, according to the insider. The elder brother was not present because he had a phobia of social gatherings and the family had not seen him for more than 10 years.
Their parents, aged 93 and 83, were unable to visit because of mobility problems. The sister’s phone records showed that she had not received WhatsApp messages from either brother since May, while the last reply from them was sent on February 18.
The sister did not live with the brothers and visited them every other month. If neither answered the door, she would usually push a handwritten letter containing cash through the letterbox and leave.
Utility bills were paid by direct debit from their father’s bank account. Electricity consumption remained at normal levels between July and August 2026. Their parents bought the 400-square-foot flat outright in 2003 for the elder brother to live in.
Inquiries with neighbours found that they had not noticed any unusual odours or noises. Although they knew that two brothers lived in the flat, they had seen only one of them leave the premises, the source said.
Neighbours also said that the brother who left the flat did not usually greet or respond to them.
According to the preliminary investigation, the younger brother is believed to have died several weeks ago, leaving the elder brother unable to care for himself. The elder brother is believed to have died this week as a result.

data.title: Hong Kong’s MTR Corp announces half-price fares for ‘Thank You Day’ on October 24
data.description:
Hong Kong’s rail operator will offer half-price fares across its network on October 24, as part of a “Thank You Day”.
The MTR Corporation said discounts would apply to Octopus and JoyYou card users on its railway, Light Rail and bus services in the northwestern New Territories, as well as to QR code ticket holders on the heavy rail network.
Cross-border journeys to and from Lo Wu and Lok Ma Chau stations on the East Rail line will also be covered.
Passengers can combine the half-price discount with interchange and fare saver discounts, a 25 per cent discount on connecting journeys under the monthly pass and the government’s HK$2 (25 US cents) fare concession scheme for elderly passengers and eligible people with disabilities.

The discount will not apply to East Rail first class, the Airport Express, MTR feeder bus services, single-journey tickets, contactless card payments or the Hong Kong section of the high-speed rail.
“The corporation will deploy additional staff at MTR stations to assist passengers and closely monitor train and station operations to suitably adjust train service and manpower arrangements when necessary,” it said.
The promotional day falls under the MTR’s service performance rebate arrangement, part of the fare adjustment mechanism, which offers discounted fares on a designated Saturday or Sunday once the rebate fund reaches HK$25 million.
Last year, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan confirmed that the corporation had been fined HK$19.2 million over a five-hour disruption on the Tseung Kwan O line in May, with the penalty allocated to passenger rebates.

data.title: Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan to set goals, not alter economic system: John Lee
data.description:
Hong Kong’s first five-year plan will include both binding and aspirational targets, the city’s leader has said, stressing that the long-term blueprint does not signal a move towards a planned economy.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu also revealed on Tuesday that the plan, which will be unveiled alongside his annual policy address the following day, would feature a blue cover symbolising “blue skies”, openness, progress and steadiness.
“There will be indicators which are binding and indicators which are anticipatory … There are things we must do and they are binding on the government particularly,” Lee told the media ahead of the top decision-making Executive Council meeting.
“And there are things we want to do very much, but we need everybody to facilitate. The government will lead, and also the government will coordinate resources, make the right policies, and everybody has to play their part in order to achieve the best result.”
But he stopped short of saying whether specific indicators would be set for major initiatives such as the Northern Metropolis megaproject.
Lee also reiterated that the plan would not alter Hong Kong’s economic system.
“I want to make it very clear: the five-year plan is not a planned economy. It is a plan which tells us where the strategic directions are, where we are heading and which are the priority areas,” Lee said.
“It is a blueprint for us to implement in five years’ time. So when we each year roll out policies, we also have to ascertain priorities so that at the end of five years we will reach certain goals.”
Lee said the theme of his fifth and final policy address of his current term would be: “A Strategic Vision for a Bright New Era; Driving Reform and Boosting Development; Unleashing Opportunities and Enhancing Livelihood”.

He said the document would retain its green cover, symbolising policy continuity, vibrancy and hope. It would also carry special significance as the first policy address to follow the announcement of the five-year plan.
“It means that we adopt a long-term perspective through the five-year plan to map out Hong Kong’s overall development, advance reforms, promote growth and create opportunities,” Lee said.
“[We will] ensure that the benefits of economic development are shared with the public, and that we embrace the future.”
Lee is scheduled to present both documents to the Legislative Council on Wednesday morning. He said they contained more than 100,000 words in total and that he would spend two to three hours outlining their key points.
The government had also prepared a summary to help the public understand the relationship between the two documents and the measures they contained, Lee added.
Authorities have said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan aims to align the city’s development more closely with the national blueprint for 2026-2030, while providing strategic direction for the years ahead.
The plan will outline the city’s vision for the metropolis, the advancement of innovation and technology, and the development of the finance, shipping and trading sectors.
The policy address will serve as a progress report on the implementation of the plan, setting out policies and advancing its direction in response to the international environment, economic forecasts and the latest developments.
The government earlier concluded a months-long public consultation on both documents. It held two town hall meetings attended by more than 200 residents and district representatives, and received more than 17,000 submissions on the five-year plan and 11,000 on the policy address.

data.title: Forms Syntron draws Hong Kong’s next-gen tycoons in HK$940 million IPO
data.description:
Hong Kong’s younger generation of tycoons is becoming increasingly active in the city’s initial public offering market through family offices and private investments. But their investments extend beyond the property and traditional financial sectors associated with their predecessors, into technology and digital finance.
Prominent business leaders Cheng Chi-heng of New World Development and Peter Lee Ka-kit of Henderson Land participated as cornerstone investors in Shenzhen Forms Syntron Information’s HK$940 million (US$119.8 million) Hong Kong listing, according to the company’s official filing on Monday.
In exchange for guaranteed share allocations and a mandatory commitment to hold the stocks for at least six months, Cheng and Lee agreed to buy HK$40 million and HK$39.6 million worth of shares, respectively. They were joined by private investment firm Thalassa Capital and Hong Kong-listed LCD manufacturer Yeebo International Holdings.
Lee has been particularly active in Hong Kong’s IPO market in recent years. Through his wholly-owned private investment vehicle, he has served as a cornerstone investor in several high-profile debuts, including XtalPi in 2024 – the first specialist technology company to list under Hong Kong’s Chapter 18C rules designed for innovative firms in hi-tech industries.
As the city’s broader IPO market stages a robust recovery in 2026 – with total funds raised surpassing HK$340 billion in the first eight months – tycoons and family offices are drawing renewed market attention.
Forms Syntron said it met these high-profile investors through business connections, introductions by corporate partners and global offering underwriters during its regular business and investment activities.

The financial technology service provider, which caters to the banking industry, has started taking investor orders for its Hong Kong listing and expects its trading debut on September 22. It is offering 58.9 million shares at a maximum price of HK$16 each, according to its listing document. The price marks a 40 per cent discount compared with the 23.02 yuan (US$3.43) closing price of its Shenzhen-listed shares on Friday.
The company plans to channel the capital raised into research and development, operational capabilities over the next three to five years, international sales expansion across mainland China and overseas markets, and potential strategic technology acquisitions.
Although headquartered in mainland China and already listed in the A-share market, Forms Syntron has strong ties to Hong Kong. Founder and chairman Chow Chi Kwan grew up and was educated in the city, earning a bachelor’s degree in social science from the Chinese University of Hong Kong in 1995. He also serves as a non-official member of Hong Kong’s Digital Economy Development Committee.
Founded in 2003, Forms Syntron provides fintech software development, consulting and systems integration services to banks, regulatory authorities and financial institutions across mainland China and Hong Kong, supporting their digital transformation.
The Hong Kong market now accounts for more than 80 per cent of the company’s total revenue. Its client base mainly comprises financial institutions and non-bank financial firms, with its top five customers contributing 89.1 per cent of revenue in 2025.
The company recorded revenue of 630 million yuan (US$93.9 million) last year, down from 740 million yuan in 2024. Full-year net profit rose 10.3 per cent year on year to 74 million yuan. The company won 221 new projects in 2025, compared with 297 in 2024.

data.title: Data from Greater Bay Area residents to help improve healthcare policy: GSK
data.description:
British pharmaceutical company GSK is turning to patient data gathered from the 88 million residents of the Greater Bay Area’s 11 cities to speed up drug development in vaccines and cancer care, as officials push for closer cross-border medical cooperation.
GSK Hong Kong and Macau general manager Nicholas Teo said patient data was very important because it could form “supplementary evidence” to support regulatory filings and potential label expansions, and also help to “discover benefits other than the medication itself”.
Vaccines were one example, Teo said last week. While their effectiveness against target diseases such as flu, shingles and respiratory syncytial virus was well established, he said researchers were increasingly studying potential benefits relating to cardiovascular health and neurological outcomes, which might help generate additional evidence and insights for future healthcare decision-making.
Teo said GSK’s expertise lay in vaccination and disease prevention, citing shingles and respiratory syncytial virus as key areas, with the viral liver infection hepatitis B another area of focus. He added that GSK also had a growing oncology and haematology portfolio.
The bay area is a government scheme aimed at integrating Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in mainland China’s Guangdong province into a single economic and business hub. Their combined gross domestic product last year was more than US$2.23 trillion, according to official data.
GSK signed a memorandum of understanding in September last year with the University of Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area International Clinical Trial Institute on a study to examine the long-term health effects of the shingles vaccine.
Teo said GSK would provide financial sponsorship for the HKU-led study and was also investing in shared data infrastructure. The company could access patient data through the partnership, such as data coming from hospitals and government agencies, but pharmaceutical companies did not have direct access to it on their own, he added.
The institute, based in the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone and set up by the Hong Kong government, enables the free exchange of researchers and data between the two cities.
Better decisions are made after we have better data
Nicholas Teo, GSK Hong Kong and Macau
The director of its real-world study and application centre, Cheung Ching-lung, said at the Hong Kong International Biotechnology Conference and Exhibition on Thursday that the institute aimed to use real-world data to drive evidence-based decision-making through global collaboration.
He said real-world data was patient data gathered during routine clinical practice at hospitals and clinics.
HKU pharmacy professor Ian Wong said at the conference that cross-border research required “infrastructure that’s safe enough” as the first pillar, alongside government regulation, ethics and public education, before real-world data could be used effectively.
Raphael Yeung, a senior pharmacist at Hong Kong’s Drug Office, said the city had multiple regulatory safeguards in place, including the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance.
Teo said the value of data ultimately came down to better outcomes and better policy.
“Better decisions are made after we have better data,” he said. “If we have data that tells you a certain medication or vaccine benefits a particular population, the government can take a decision on whether to make it available, subsidise it, or improve access.”
Teo added that GSK wanted to help prove that the cross-border data pipeline could work at scale.
“We hope to be part of potential pilot studies or collaborations that will prove this data flow is safe, secure and high quality between Hong Kong and mainland China,” he said.

data.title: Hong Kong leader vows accountability over faulty lifts at Queen Mary Hospital
data.description:
Hong Kong authorities will hold construction firms and government personnel accountable for faulty lift installation work at Queen Mary Hospital’s new block, the city’s leader has said, as he tasked the Development Bureau with submitting a report within a month.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday that he had instructed the bureau, which had given him a preliminary briefing, to “thoroughly investigate the matter and report within a month”.
“We will pursue accountability, including contractors, subcontractors, engineering personnel and professionals. And if there are government personnel involved, we will pursue their accountability as well,” he said ahead of his meeting with the Executive Council. “We also need to identify where and whether the system has any inadequacies and rectify them.
“To consider what further action we will do, we must first find very clearly about what happened, where are the inadequacies, and whether any person who should be held accountable, we should pursue their accountability. After we have found out the facts, then we will decide what further steps we shall take.”

Lee’s comments came a month after defective work at the hospital – the largest on Hong Kong Island – came under scrutiny, with 24 of the 28 lifts in its new 34-storey clinical block deemed unfit for use.
Sources previously told the South China Morning Post that Li Pak-yee, a chief project manager at the Architectural Services Department who oversaw the development, had been asked to resign and left her post over the scandal.
The department denied that there had been any “forced resignation”, saying Li had quit for “personal reasons” after giving three months’ notice.
Lee did not directly address the SCMP’s questions about whether the resignation would affect the investigation and why the government had not invoked its “Heads of Department Accountability System”, proposed in his policy address last year to improve governance.
He stressed that medical services were important to the public and that the new block should open as soon as possible.
Widespread installation defects, revealed last month, have delayed the full commissioning of the hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year, raising serious concerns over project oversight and civil service accountability.

data.title: In Focus|Cast out: why China’s young workers see sacking saga as sign of unsettling timesThe outlook for China’s young jobseekers could worsen further, after an ugly fallout from Xingyu’s mass dismiss
data.description:
Weeks after sparking a nationwide outcry over its mass dismissal of recent college graduates, Xingyu – a major automotive lighting maker in eastern China – has severely penalised four of its executives and promised to help the former employees find new jobs.
Two of the firm’s top executives received salary deductions and two human resources managers were dismissed or demoted for their “misjudgment and hasty decision-making”, the company said in a lengthy statement detailing its recent “mistake” last week.
The saga began in early August, when the Shanghai-listed company, whose clients include international carmakers such as Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, presented more than 370 fresh graduates – who had joined the company a month earlier – with a stark choice.
They could either resign “voluntarily” and receive half a month’s salary, or stay and be reassigned from office-based technical roles to factory-floor work, including tightening screws.
According to the firm, 107 chose the former option. But the uproar that ensued has placed the company firmly in the centre of a media firestorm, with Communist Party news organ People’s Daily calling the move “a blatant trampling of social trust” in a commentary late last month.
The extensive public attention the incident aroused stood as a tangible reflection of corporate workforce contraction, youth employment pressure and growing incidents of labour disputes, phenomena occurring within a broader slowdown in the world’s second-largest economy, analysts said.
While neither the firm nor local authorities specified any violation of labour law by the short-term manoeuvre, which coincided with its application for a listing in Hong Kong, its adverse effects were evident, the analysts warned.
“The company’s planned Hong Kong listing is very likely to be blocked, because the negative impact is simply too damaging,” said Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank in Beijing.
As for the employment of fresh graduates – an increasingly sensitive issue for Beijing amid a tough job market – “the fact that this incident has escalated to such a degree is also highly unfavourable. Big companies will become very cautious in their future hiring”, he said.
According to its statement, Xingyu had recruited more than 400 college graduates through campus hiring last autumn and this spring, while 372 formally joined the company in July.


About one month into their employment, the company’s human resources department conducted one-on-one meetings with each of them, presenting the binary choice. The decision resulted from a workforce optimisation plan “based on the company’s order pipeline and staffing needs”, it said.
The move sparked backlash from many former employees, who complained to domestic media that after being dismissed, they lost their status as fresh graduates and could only re-enter the job market as social hires with a termination record on their résumés.
Within China’s institutional framework, losing this status stripped them of many competitive job-seeking advantages.
The company and the municipal human resources bureau of Changzhou, where Xingyu is based, have so far arranged for 71 of those dismissed to join new employers, while an additional 22 passed interviews and received offer letters.
The remainder were either undertaking interviews or planning to pursue postgraduate studies, Xingyu said last week.
Previously, both the firm and the bureau responded with apologies and explanations over the incident but failed to quell widespread public scepticism.
On August 25, the bureau confirmed the controversial lay-off – after media reports went viral – noting that the negotiation process was “overly rigid and simplistic, lacking full and effective communication”.
Two days later, the firm issued a public apology, acknowledging “managerial errors in decision-making” and offering a package of remedies including three months’ worth of job-seeking living allowances, free dormitory accommodation and an additional six months’ salary compensation for those who remained unemployed.
At its half-year performance briefing on September 2, the company’s chairwoman and general manager, Zhou Xiaoping, apologised and said the company was “properly implementing remedial measures” under government guidance.
According to its earnings results, Xingyu posted revenue of 6.88 billion yuan (US$1 billion) in the first half of the year, up 1.87 per cent, year on year, with a profit of about 712 million yuan, down 7.78 per cent, year on year.
Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard
Nie Riming, Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law
Its 2025 sales figures showed that it held an 11.6 per cent share of China’s automotive lighting market, ranking first in the country, and accounted for 4.6 per cent of the global market share, ranking seventh.
Nie Riming, a researcher at the Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law, said the broader lacklustre job market was primarily why this incident generated such a huge response.
“Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard,” he said.
Another record-breaking army of university graduates – an estimated 12.7 million students – entered China’s job market this summer, up about 4 per cent from last year, according to official data. The youth jobless rate – covering those aged 16 to 24, excluding students – climbed to 17.9 per cent in July from 14.9 per cent in the previous month.
Nie noted that Xingyu’s immediate cash compensation alone could compare favourably with statutory minimums in Germany, where labour protections are generally stronger.
While China has relatively high-standard labour laws on paper, enforcement and compliance are uneven, especially among smaller firms, he said. Against this backdrop, listed companies like Xingyu – along with foreign-invested firms and state-owned enterprises – remain the primary sources of higher-quality jobs in China.
However, these relatively “well-behaved” companies had been steadily reducing their headcount in recent years, and after this incident, such formal, regulated positions were likely to become even more scarce, he added.
“For companies going forward, they will become increasingly cautious when hiring for compliant, formal positions,” he said.
“They will lean more towards non-standard employment arrangements – such as outsourcing and dispatching – to offload their staffing responsibilities. That, in turn, would further reduce formal direct hiring and reinforce labour-market dualisation.”
The most contentious issue remains fresh graduate status, as many recruitment policies, including those for civil service admissions, favour fresh graduates, he said.


“The way graduates are regulated has yet to align with the job market, and this disconnect must be resolved before it causes further frustration,” he urged.
As the economic slowdown persists in China, lay-offs have become a recurring theme in the workplace, and labour disputes are on the rise.
Labour dispute mediation and arbitration bodies at all levels handled 4.54 million cases nationwide in 2025 – a 7 per cent increase from 2024, following a 10 per cent rise over 2023, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security’s annual statistical bulletin.
Meanwhile, Xingyu’s lay-off controversy emerged after it refiled its updated H-share listing application with the Hong Kong stock exchange at the end of July, sparking market speculation that it was a short-term tactic to pad the company’s research workforce and make it look stronger for its listing ambitions.
Among the dismissed employees, about two-thirds held bachelor’s degrees, while the remainder held master’s degrees. The majority were assigned to research and development roles, as well as manufacturing and production positions, while a smaller number were allocated functional support roles, according to last week’s statement.
However, legal experts and academics considered it unlikely that this was the company’s primary intention, given that such a move would offer limited substantive gain while exposing it to significant compliance and reputational risks.
Such risks may soon materialise, such as hindering its listing progress, said Zhao Zhanling, a commercial lawyer from Beijing-based Javy Law Firm.
“The stock exchange and its advisers are likely to demand clarifications on the mass lay-offs, labour law compliance and internal control mechanisms,” he said. “Adverse media coverage may also invite regulatory questions, causing delays – though not necessarily scuttling the IPO altogether.”
The Shanghai Stock Exchange website showed that it issued a regulatory work letter to Xingyu on Wednesday, specifying regulatory requirements regarding the company’s “relevant matters”, without providing further details.
The saga could also lead to a loss of business opportunities, according to Tang, the Beijing researcher.
“It is possible that its international clients would respond positively to public outcry,” he said, “but that does not mean they would punish Xingyu – they may downgrade its supplier tier ... or impose more stringent supply conditions.”
Volkswagen China said earlier this month that it had initiated an investigation into the matter following intense media coverage.
